subject: computer-science
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Which right under the UK GDPR allows an individual to obtain their personal data in a structured, commonly used, machine-readable format and transfer it to another controller?
options: The right to restrict processing
The right to object
The right to rectification
The right to data portability
questions.explain: The right to data portability lets a data subject receive and reuse their data across services in a machine-readable format.

questions.q: The 'data minimisation' principle of the UK GDPR requires that personal data collected is:
options: Shared with as many partners as possible
Adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary for the purpose
Stored only on UK servers
Encrypted using asymmetric algorithms
questions.explain: Data minimisation means collecting only the personal data that is adequate, relevant and necessary for the stated purpose.

questions.q: A serious ethical objection to opaque ('black box') algorithmic decision-making in areas like sentencing or recruitment is that:
options: It always produces random results
It is illegal under the Copyright Act
It uses asymmetric encryption
Affected individuals cannot easily understand, challenge or hold anyone accountable for the decision
questions.explain: Lack of transparency makes it hard to explain, contest or assign responsibility for automated decisions, undermining accountability.

questions.q: The Regulation of Investigatory Powers Act (RIPA) is mainly concerned with:
options: Criminalising the creation of malware
Setting rules for storing personal data
Regulating surveillance and the interception of communications by authorities
Protecting copyright of software
questions.explain: RIPA governs how public bodies may carry out surveillance and intercept communications.

questions.q: When a machine-learning model used for loan approval is trained on historical lending decisions, the principal ethical risk is that it may:
options: Use too little electricity
Reproduce and entrench past discrimination present in the training data
Run too slowly to be useful
Refuse to make any decisions at all
questions.explain: Models trained on biased historical data can learn and perpetuate the discrimination embedded in that data.

questions.q: The Computer Misuse Act 1990 created an offence of unauthorised access made 'with intent to commit or facilitate a further offence'. This is best described as:
options: Identical in penalty to basic unauthorised access
A more serious offence than simple unauthorised access, carrying heavier penalties
A civil matter only, not criminal
An offence only if data is actually stolen
questions.explain: The second Computer Misuse Act offence (access with intent to commit further crimes) is treated more seriously than basic unauthorised access.

questions.q: Under the Computer Misuse Act 1990, which of the following is an offence?
options: Storing personal data without encryption
Gaining unauthorised access to computer material
Copying software you have legally purchased
Failing to keep data accurate
questions.explain: The Computer Misuse Act 1990 makes unauthorised access to computer systems a criminal offence.

questions.q: The Regulation of Investigatory Powers Act 2000 differs from the Computer Misuse Act 1990 in that RIPA chiefly:
options: Governs lawful interception and surveillance of communications by authorities
Criminalises writing malware
Protects original creative works
Defines the data protection principles
questions.explain: RIPA regulates how public bodies may lawfully intercept communications and conduct surveillance, a separate concern from the hacking offences in the Computer Misuse Act.

questions.q: A key practical difference between proprietary and open-source licensing for a business is that open-source software typically:
options: Removes all need for technical support
Always costs more than proprietary equivalents
Cannot legally be used commercially
Allows the source code to be inspected and modified, but may impose obligations such as sharing changes
questions.explain: Open-source licences grant access to and modification of the source, but licences like the GPL can require sharing modifications, unlike closed proprietary software.

questions.q: Government-mandated filtering or blocking of websites raises an ethical tension chiefly between:
options: Volume and velocity of data
Protecting people from harm and the right to freedom of expression and access to information
Symmetric and asymmetric keys
Patents and copyright
questions.explain: Internet censorship balances protection from harmful content against rights to free expression and access to information.

questions.q: Beyond manufacturing and e-waste, a growing environmental concern about large-scale computing, especially data centres and AI training, is their:
options: Tendency to reduce global electricity demand
Reliance on open-source software
High energy consumption and associated carbon emissions and water use for cooling
Inability to be networked
questions.explain: Large data centres and AI training consume substantial energy and cooling resources, raising carbon and sustainability concerns.

questions.q: The 'digital divide' refers to:
options: The difference between analogue and digital signals
The inequality between those with and without access to digital technology and the internet
The split between symmetric and asymmetric encryption
The gap between fast and slow processors
questions.explain: The digital divide is the gap in access to and ability to use digital technology, often along economic or geographic lines.

questions.q: Under GDPR, an individual's 'right to be forgotten' allows them to:
options: Demand a copy of all source code
Request that their personal data be erased under certain conditions
Bypass a firewall legally
Avoid paying for software licences
questions.explain: GDPR grants individuals the right to have their personal data erased in specified circumstances.

questions.q: Under the UK GDPR, which role describes the entity that determines the purposes and means of processing personal data?
options: The data subject
The data processor
The data controller
The Information Commissioner
questions.explain: The data controller decides why and how personal data is processed, whereas a processor merely acts on the controller's instructions.

questions.q: A BCS member is offered a contract requiring expertise they clearly do not possess. The Code of Conduct expects them to:
options: Decline all future work in that field
Subcontract secretly without telling the client
Accept it anyway to gain experience
Only undertake work within their professional competence, or gain/acquire the needed competence
questions.explain: The BCS Code requires members to work only within their professional competence and to be honest about their limitations.

questions.q: The Data Protection Act / GDPR primarily governs:
options: Unauthorised hacking of systems
The collection, storage and processing of personal data
The interception of communications
The copying of software
questions.explain: Data protection legislation regulates how organisations collect, store and process individuals' personal data.

questions.q: Under the UK GDPR, the data subject's 'right of access' (a subject access request) entitles an individual to:
options: Delete any company's database
Demand the source code of the processing software
Prevent the company from trading
Obtain confirmation of and a copy of the personal data an organisation holds about them
questions.explain: A subject access request lets an individual obtain confirmation that their data is being processed and a copy of it.

questions.q: Intellectual property protection through patents is intended to:
options: Make all inventions free to copy immediately
Give inventors exclusive rights to their invention for a limited period
Regulate the interception of communications
Prevent anyone from ever using an invention
questions.explain: A patent grants an inventor exclusive commercial rights for a limited time, encouraging innovation.

questions.q: Which statement best reflects a core duty in the BCS Code of Conduct?
options: Maximise personal profit above all else
Never share knowledge with junior colleagues
Have due regard for public health, privacy, security and the wellbeing of others and the environment
Accept any work regardless of competence
questions.explain: The BCS Code of Conduct requires members to act in the public interest, including regard for health, privacy, security and the environment.

questions.q: Algorithmic bias in AI systems most commonly arises from:
options: Running the model on a faster network
Encrypting the training data
Using too much computing power
Training on data that reflects existing human or historical prejudices
questions.explain: AI can learn and amplify biases present in its training data, leading to unfair outcomes.

questions.q: A major cultural/global impact of dominant computing platforms and online services originating in a few countries is:
options: The complete elimination of all languages
Guaranteed equal access for everyone worldwide
Concerns over cultural homogenisation and the underrepresentation of minority languages and viewpoints online
The removal of the digital divide
questions.explain: Globally dominant platforms can promote cultural homogenisation and leave minority languages and cultures underrepresented.

questions.q: The GNU General Public Licence (GPL) is described as 'copyleft' because it requires that:
options: The original author retains sole rights to modify it
The software must be sold, never given away
Source code must always be kept secret
Derivative works distributed to others must also be released under the same open licence
questions.explain: The GPL's copyleft condition requires that redistributed derivative works remain under the same free licence, keeping the source open.

questions.q: Electronic waste (e-waste) is an environmental concern mainly because:
options: It only affects software companies
Discarded devices contain toxic materials and are often not recycled responsibly
It improves recycling rates automatically
It reduces the demand for raw materials
questions.explain: E-waste contains hazardous substances and rare materials, posing pollution and sustainability problems when discarded.

questions.q: An employee uses a colleague's password, which they guessed, simply to read files out of curiosity, copying nothing. Under the Computer Misuse Act 1990 this is:
options: Only a breach of the Copyright Act
The basic offence of unauthorised access to computer material
Not an offence because nothing was copied
Lawful if no damage results
questions.explain: Merely securing unauthorised access to computer material is itself the first Computer Misuse Act offence, regardless of whether data is copied.

questions.q: Which of the following is one of the data protection principles set out in the UK GDPR / Data Protection Act 2018?
options: Data accuracy is the responsibility of the data subject alone
Data must be processed lawfully, fairly and in a transparent manner
Data may be kept indefinitely for any future purpose
Data subjects have no right to see their own data
questions.explain: The first principle requires personal data to be processed lawfully, fairly and transparently.

questions.q: The Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988 protects:
options: Personal data held by companies
Networks against denial-of-service attacks
Individuals from unlawful surveillance
Original works such as software, music and writing from being copied without permission
questions.explain: This Act protects intellectual property, making unauthorised copying of original works unlawful.

questions.q: The Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988 differs from a software licence in that the Act:
options: Only applies to music, not software
Sets the price the software must be sold at
Replaces the need for any licence
Establishes the underlying legal right of the creator, while the licence specifies how others may use the work
questions.explain: The Act grants the creator's automatic copyright, whereas a licence is the agreement defining how others may lawfully use the protected work.

questions.q: Which best illustrates a breach of the UK GDPR 'storage limitation' principle?
options: Encrypting customer records at rest
Letting customers correct inaccurate data
Deleting data once it is no longer needed
Keeping customers' personal data forever with no review, long after the purpose has ended
questions.explain: Storage limitation requires personal data to be kept no longer than necessary for the purpose for which it was processed.

questions.q: Which scenario constitutes the third offence under the Computer Misuse Act 1990 (unauthorised acts impairing operation)?
options: Reading a file you are permitted to view
Buying a second copy of legitimate software
Requesting your own data from a company
Releasing a virus designed to delete files and disrupt a system
questions.explain: The third offence covers unauthorised acts intended to impair the operation of a computer, such as deploying malware.

questions.q: A cloud company that only stores and handles personal data strictly on behalf of another organisation, following its instructions, is acting as the:
options: Data processor
Data subject
Supervisory authority
Data controller
questions.explain: A data processor processes personal data on behalf of, and under the instructions of, the controller.
